newsitem.title: DUBAI: HORSE RACING-DUBAI WORLD CUP CALLED OFF AFTER DESERT FLOOD.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-DUBAI WORLD CUP CALLED OFF AFTER DESERT FLOOD.

text.p: A thunderstorm and flash flood forced organisers to call off Saturday's $4 million Dubai World Cup, a glittering showpiece in this Arab emirate's ambition to be the sporting capital of the Middle East.
The decision was made by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum, host of the world's richest horse race and the world's most successful owner-breeder.
He had watched gloomily as torrential rain had fallen at Dubai's Nad al-Sheba race course on the outskirts of the city since early afternoon.

After walking on the water-logged sand track and discussing the situation with trainers of the 13 thoroughbreds chasing a $2.4 million first prize, he sent race committee official Brough Scott to announce: "The race is off tonight."
Sheikh Mohammed was discussing whether the race could be held next week but Scott said it was clear the track would not be in racing condition for many days.
Large tracts of desert were already awash from a heavy but less intense storm on Tuesday night which had kept the dirt track sealed until Friday morning and interfered with the training schedule.
Scott said shortly before the decision that a race could have been run on the track if the rain had stopped.
"The snag is, you might not be able to find it," he said.

Officials said the six-race meeting cost about $10 million to stage and had been due to be watched by a crowd of 30,000 people, including international show business celebrities, at the track on the outskirts of this usually blistering hot Gulf city.
Millions more racing fans in Europe, Asia and North America had been expected to tune in to satellite television casts.
"I've been in Dubai working on this since the beginning of the month," said one racing official from Britain. "We must try to keep smiling but I'm thinking of opening a bottle of scotch."
The big race, which drew horses from Europe, the United States, Brazil, Australia and Japan, had been due to be run under floodlights at 8.15 p.m. (1615 GMT).

Among the contenders were U.S.-trained dirt horses Siphon, winner of the Santa Anita Handicap, and Sandpit, Siphon's stable mate. They were both bred in Brazil and favoured to make it another U.S. win following last year's triumph by wonderhorse Cigar.
European champion Helissio, winner of last year's Prix de L'Arc de Triomphe, and Japan Cup winner Singspiel were the favoured horses from Europe.
